question: If two dice are tossed, the probability that the product of the numbers showing on the tops of the dice is greater than \(10\) is
solution:
Use the conventional model of two independent fair six-sided dice, each numbered \(1\) through \(6\). Label them first and second so that each ordered result is counted separately. There are \(6\cdot6=36\) equally likely results.

For each first-die value, list the second-die values that make the product greater than \(10\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
1&:\ \text{none},\\
2&:\ 6,\\
3&:\ 4,5,6,\\
4&:\ 3,4,5,6,\\
5&:\ 3,4,5,6,\\
6&:\ 2,3,4,5,6.
\end{aligned}
\]
For example, when the first die shows \(2\), a second-die value of \(5\) gives exactly \(10\), so only \(6\) qualifies. Each ordered result belongs to exactly one first-die case, making the list exhaustive without duplication.

The number of favorable results is
\[
0+1+3+4+4+5=17.
\]
Thus the probability is \(\boxed{\frac{17}{36}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
